blocks.text: One of the oldest interspecific forms of cooperation

Teamwork between humans and dogs is one of the oldest and best-documented interspecific forms of cooperation. It is based on mutual benefit, reliable communication and learned coordination. Its origins lie in the domestication of the wolf (Canis lupus), which according to current research began approximately 15,000 to at least 30,000 years ago, possibly in several regions independently of one another.

Today this cooperation is applied in very different contexts, including hunting, herding, rescue and search work, assistance and therapy settings, and in everyday life as social companionship. In technical terms it can be described as an interplay of behavioural-biological adaptations, learning-psychological processes, emotional bonding and cultural-ethical framework conditions.
This relationship is not a dominance relationship in the ethological sense, but a functional cooperation with asymmetrical responsibility .
Humans control resources and living conditions, while dogs have highly developed social adaptations to humans. This results in both special capability and clear ethical obligations.
Behavioural biology and cognition
Evolutionary foundations 🧬

Social cognition: Compared with other non-human mammals, dogs show exceptional abilities in social cognition towards humans. These include reliably following human pointing gestures, interpreting gaze direction and adapting to human emotional signals.

Cooperation check: Our experience shows that dogs can distinguish between cooperative and non-cooperative people after only a few observations. This ability is in principle universal, but shows individual and breed-specific differences.
Domestication effect: These abilities do not arise through training alone, but are based on selection effects resulting from domestication and are therefore genetically anchored.
Biology of bonding 🔬

Oxytocin: Social interactions between humans and dogs can be accompanied by measurable neuroendocrine effects. Studies show that mutual eye contact or empathic touch can be associated with an increase in oxytocin in both partners. A reciprocal oxytocin feedback loop is established, which functionally has parallels to bonding mechanisms between human caregivers.

Neural synchronisation: One can assume temporary neural synchronisation between human and dog during calm social interactions (e.g. stroking, calm eye contact). This is thought to involve shared states of attention and affect, which however probably occur only in controlled situations.

Practical applications: In working contexts (e.g. assistance, police or rescue dogs), the performance of a team depends substantially on the fit between the human personality and the dog's personality, the quality of training and the way the relationship is shaped. For humans, positive effects on mental health and, as a consequence, on physical constitution can be observed.
Welfare risks ⚠️

Functionalising dogs can be associated with welfare risks, in particular with inadequate husbandry, overburdening or purely utility-oriented selection that disregards the individual needs of the dog. We must be aware at all times of our great responsibility towards the dogs living in our care.

In addition, different genetic lines and working types (e.g. hunting, protection, guarding, herding, companion dogs, etc.) require adapted training and husbandry conditions as well as specifically adapted forms of cooperation. Before acquiring a dog, we must be absolutely clear about these specific challenges.
Emotional bonding and co-regulation
Emotional co-regulation 💚

Secure base: Our dogs react sensitively to human emotional states and show behaviours that could be interpreted as emotion-regulating (e.g. seeking closeness, establishing body contact, retrieving previously learned communication patterns). Dogs see us as a secure base, following patterns similar to those of interpersonal bonds.
Stress reduction: Physical contact, such as calm stroking, is associated with a reduction in physiological stress markers (cortisol) in both partners. These effects are lastingly repeatable.

Delimitation: Co-regulation between humans and dogs is naturally subject to limits, since, owing to the lack of verbal exchange of thoughts, co-regulation can only take place on a physical and emotional level.
Modern relationship building

Options for action: Sustainable teamwork requires that dogs have options for action within clear boundaries. Concepts such as choices in training or the voluntary initiation of interactions are increasingly regarded as promoting welfare.

Dominance myth: Classical dominance models are considered inadequate in modern behavioural research, as they oversimplify complex social dynamics and do not adequately describe the actual nature of the human-dog relationship.
Ethics, friendship and responsibility
Friendship & ethics 📚

Friendship: Over 2,000 years ago, Aristotle already studied friendship intensively and distinguished three kinds: useful friendship, which is based on advantage; pleasure-oriented friendship, which mainly seeks fun and enjoyment; and, as the highest and true form, friendship between virtuous people who genuinely strengthen and support each other in what is good. We experience this deep kind of friendship every day with our dog as a loyal, unconditional companion who is always with us without ifs and buts and who is attached to us with a naturalness that is rarely found in people. Schopenhauer recognised that a dog's loyalty is such a precious gift that it creates at least as much moral obligation towards us as friendship with another person.

Against the mechanistic view: Dogs feel joy, fear and affection, and show genuine compassion. They are not "things", but sentient, social beings who actively live with us and with whom we are meant to understand each other.

Empathic equality: Our relationship with the dog is not one of equals. We humans decide about breeding, husbandry, food and walks, and our dog cannot take part in the decision. In doing so we unfortunately still remain within the realm of speciesism, that is, a kind of discrimination in favour of one's own species. The solution does not mean that dogs must have the same rights as humans, but it demands of us a particularly high level of responsibility with regard to living together. We must not see them merely as a useful pet or a pastime, but must keep their welfare in view as seriously as if our own welfare were at stake.
Teamwork between humans and dogs is best understood within a biopsychosocial model that integrates biological foundations, emotional processes and ethical reflection.
A functioning human-dog cooperation is neither romantic equality nor authoritarian control, but a structured partnership whose quality depends on knowledge, empathy and ethical self-reflection.
The human-dog relationship is based on cooperation, not on authoritarian dominance.
Dogs are evolutionarily specialised in interpreting human signals and have exceptional social abilities in this respect.
Oxytocin plays an important role and strengthens the social bond in both humans and dogs.
Emotional co-regulation improves the wellbeing of both partners and lowers physiological stress markers.
The asymmetrical distribution of power requires increased ethical reflection and responsibility.
Knowledge + empathy + ethical self-reflection = a successful team.
